To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) stimulating parenting was negatively correlated with living in an Indigenous community, and 2) living in an Indigenous Community was associated with significantly higher stimulating parenting among Indigenous families than in non-Indigenous communities.

stimulating parenting was associated with child sex, age, socio-emotional development, maternal age and education, household crowding, and living in a nonindigenous community, but not with household poverty, father’s residential status, community marginalization, or community indigenous population.

(a) stimulating parenting was negatively and positively associated with living in a non-Indigenous community and living in an Indigenous community, respectively; (b) living in an Indigenous or non-Indigenous was associated with stimulating parenting among Indigenous families only; (c) maternal education was associated with stimulating practices only in Indigenous communities; and (d) household crowding was associated with stimulating only in non-Indigenous communities
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of parenting in the development and transmission of poverty across generations.
the development of a new approach to the problem of parenting practices in the context of a new approach.
understanding the role of ethnicity and poverty in shaping parenting practices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parenting practices are influenced by ethnicity, marginalization, education and poverty and that these factors may interact in ways that may compromise or support parenting.
living in an indigenous rural Mexican community is associated with more stimulating parenting practices among indigenous mothers.
living in an indigenous Mexican community is associated with lower levels of stimulating parenting among non-indigenous families; and higher levels of stimulating parenting for indigenous families.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stimulating parenting is more common in non-indigenous than indigenous communities.

living in an indigenous Mexican community is a significant protective factor for indigenous mothers’ parenting practices; but that poverty; education; and household crowing are significant risk factors for parenting practices among non-indigenous mothers in Mexican communities.
living in indigenous communities and having higher education are associated with stimulating parenting practices.
The main takeaway from our work is that

living in an indigenous context may be a protective factor for stimulating parenting practices in indigenous mothers; however; living in a nonindigenous context may be detrimental for these practices in indigenous families.
the effects of poverty and community marginalization on parenting practices are not universal; and may be moderated by ethnicity; education; and household crowing.
the effects of ethnicity; marginalization and poverty on stimulating parenting practices may be context-specific; and may be moderated by maternal education and household crowding.
